label: Geography: set 3 (agriculture, mining, industry, energy, transport, trade, environment, Sierra Leone)

papers.title: Agriculture as an Economic Activity: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on agriculture as an economic activity, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In shifting cultivation, the farmer
questions.explanation:
Land is cleared by slash and burn, farmed for two or three years, then abandoned for a new area.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- uses fertilisers to farm the same plot every year: That is permanent cultivation.
- rears cattle in search of pasture: That is pastoral nomadism.
- grows one cash crop on a large estate: That is plantation agriculture.

options.label: A
options.content: moves to a new piece of land when the soil becomes exhausted

options.label: B
options.content: uses fertilisers to farm the same plot every year

options.label: C
options.content: rears cattle in search of pasture

options.label: D
options.content: grows one cash crop on a large estate

questions.stem: Bush fallowing differs from shifting cultivation because in bush fallowing
questions.explanation:
Farmers stay in one village and return to plots after a fallow period.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the land is never left to rest: Bush fallowing depends on resting the land.
- crops are grown only for export: Bush fallowing is mainly for food.
- machines are used to clear the land: Clearing is usually by cutlass and fire.

options.label: A
options.content: the land is never left to rest

options.label: B
options.content: the village is permanent and only the farm plots are rotated

options.label: C
options.content: crops are grown only for export

options.label: D
options.content: machines are used to clear the land

questions.stem: Plantation agriculture is the
questions.explanation:
Examples are rubber at Harbel in Liberia and oil palm estates in Pujehun District, Sierra Leone.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- growing of food crops by a family for its own use: That is subsistence farming.
- rearing of animals by moving herds from place to place: That is pastoral nomadism.
- growing of crops and rearing of animals on the same farm: That is mixed farming.

options.label: A
options.content: growing of food crops by a family for its own use

options.label: B
options.content: rearing of animals by moving herds from place to place

options.label: C
options.content: growing of a single cash crop on a large estate, mainly for export

options.label: D
options.content: growing of crops and rearing of animals on the same farm

questions.stem: Pastoral nomadism in West Africa is practised mainly by the
questions.explanation:
Fulani herders move cattle across the savanna and Sahel in search of water and pasture.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Mende: The Mende are mainly crop farmers in southern Sierra Leone.
- Ashanti: The Ashanti of Ghana are known for cocoa farming.
- Igbo: The Igbo of south-eastern Nigeria are mainly crop farmers and traders.

questions.stem: The Office du Niger in Mali is an example of
questions.explanation:
It uses water from the River Niger's inland delta to grow rice and sugar cane.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a cocoa plantation: Cocoa does not grow in the dry Sahel of Mali.
- a mining company: It is an agricultural scheme.
- a fishing port: Mali is landlocked.

papers.title: Mining and Mineral Resources: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on mining and mineral resources, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The method of mining in which the overburden is removed and the mineral is dug from a large pit is
questions.explanation:
Open-cast mining is used for large deposits near the surface, such as iron ore at Tonkolili.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- shaft mining: Shaft mining reaches deep deposits through tunnels.
- alluvial mining: Alluvial mining washes minerals from river gravels.
- drilling: Drilling is used for oil and gas.

questions.stem: Alluvial mining is the recovery of minerals from
questions.explanation:
Most of Sierra Leone's diamonds are dug, washed and sieved from river gravels.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- deep veins reached by shafts: That is underground mining.
- oil wells beneath the sea: That is drilling.
- the overburden of an open pit: Overburden is waste rock removed to reach a deposit.

options.label: C
options.content: sand and gravel deposited by rivers

options.label: D
options.content: the overburden of an open pit

questions.stem: The West African country with some of the largest bauxite reserves in the world is
questions.explanation:
Guinea's bauxite is mined around Boké and exported for aluminium production.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Niger: Niger is known for uranium.
- Nigeria: Nigeria is known for petroleum.
- Mauritania: Mauritania is known for iron ore.

questions.stem: Iron ore from Tonkolili in Sierra Leone is exported through the port of
questions.explanation:
A railway carries the ore from Tonkolili to Pepel on the Sierra Leone River estuary.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Nitti: Nitti exports rutile.
- Bonthe: Bonthe is a small island port in the south.
- Kambia: Kambia is an inland town in the north-west.

questions.stem: The Kimberley Process Certification Scheme aims to
questions.explanation:
Launched in 2003, it requires certificates showing that traded diamonds are not from conflict zones.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- increase the price of gold: It deals with diamonds, not gold prices.
- train miners in Sierra Leone: It is a certification scheme, not training.
- ban all diamond mining in Africa: It certifies diamonds; it does not ban mining.

options.label: B
options.content: stop the trade in conflict (blood) diamonds

options.label: D
options.content: ban all diamond mining in Africa

papers.title: Manufacturing Industries: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on manufacturing industries, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: An industry whose raw materials lose much weight during processing is usually located
questions.explanation:
Processing near the source, as with cement or sugar, avoids paying to transport waste.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- near its market: Market location suits industries that gain weight.
- anywhere, as it is footloose: Footloose industries use light inputs.
- only at a seaport: A port is not essential for weight-losing industries.

questions.stem: Breweries are usually located near their markets because
questions.explanation:
Brewing is weight-gaining, so it is cheapest to produce near customers, as at Wellington, Freetown.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- their raw materials are perishable: The raw materials (grain, hops) are not the main reason.
- they need very large amounts of electricity: Brewing is not power-intensive like smelting.
- they use imported machinery: Machinery does not decide location.

options.label: B
options.content: they need very large amounts of electricity

options.label: D
options.content: the finished product is heavy and bulky, as water is added

questions.stem: The aluminium smelter at Tema in Ghana was located there mainly because of
questions.explanation:
Aluminium smelting needs huge amounts of electricity, supplied by the Akosombo scheme.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- local deposits of iron ore: Aluminium is made from bauxite, not iron ore.
- a large local market for aluminium: The market was not the main factor.
- cheap coal from Enugu: Enugu coal is in Nigeria, and smelting used hydroelectricity.

options.label: A
options.content: cheap hydroelectric power from the Akosombo Dam

options.label: C
options.content: a large local market for aluminium

questions.stem: A footloose industry is one that
questions.explanation:
Electronics and software, with light, valuable inputs and products, are footloose.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- must be located beside its raw materials: That is a raw-material-oriented industry.
- moves its factory from town to town: Footloose does not mean the factory moves.
- depends on heavy, bulky inputs: Heavy inputs tie an industry to its raw materials.

options.label: A
options.content: must be located beside its raw materials

options.label: B
options.content: is not tied to raw materials or markets and can locate almost anywhere

options.label: C
options.content: moves its factory from town to town

questions.stem: Import substitution means
questions.explanation:
It saves foreign exchange and creates jobs in local industry.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- exporting manufactured goods: That is export promotion.
- banning all imports: Import substitution does not mean banning all imports.
- replacing local goods with imported ones: That is the opposite.

options.label: C
options.content: producing at home goods that were formerly imported

options.label: D
options.content: replacing local goods with imported ones

papers.title: Energy and Power: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on energy and power, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a renewable source of energy?
questions.explanation:
Renewable sources such as sunlight, water and wind are replaced naturally.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- coal: Coal is a fossil fuel and will run out.
- petroleum: Petroleum is non-renewable.
- natural gas: Natural gas is non-renewable.

questions.stem: Which is an important physical condition for hydroelectric power development?
questions.explanation:
HEP needs plenty of water flowing all year, a good fall and a narrow valley with hard rock.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a large local population: A market is a human condition.
- soft, porous rocks for the dam: Dams need hard, impermeable rock.
- a wide, flat valley at the dam site: A narrow gorge is best for the dam itself.

options.label: A
options.content: a large and regular volume of water

options.label: C
options.content: soft, porous rocks for the dam

options.label: D
options.content: a wide, flat valley at the dam site

questions.stem: The Akosombo Dam is built across the
questions.explanation:
Akosombo, completed in 1965, created Lake Volta in Ghana.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- River Niger: Kainji is on the Niger.
- River Senegal: Manantali is on a tributary of the Senegal.
- Seli River: Bumbuna is on the Seli.

questions.stem: The Bumbuna hydroelectric dam in Sierra Leone is on the
questions.explanation:
Bumbuna, in Tonkolili District, began supplying power in 2009.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Moa River: The Moa flows through the east past Tiwai Island.
- Sewa River: The Sewa flows through the centre and south.
- Mano River: The Mano forms part of the Liberian border.

questions.stem: A disease that often spreads around the reservoirs of hydroelectric dams is
questions.explanation:
The snails that carry bilharzia breed in the still water of reservoirs and irrigation channels.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- measles: Measles spreads from person to person through the air.
- tuberculosis: Tuberculosis is not linked to still water.
- diabetes: Diabetes is not an infectious disease.

papers.title: Transportation: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on transportation, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The cheapest way of moving bulky goods over long distances is by
questions.explanation:
Ships carry very large loads cheaply, though slowly.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- air transport: Air is the most expensive mode.
- road transport: Road is costly for bulky loads over long distances.
- motorbike taxis: These carry only light loads over short distances.

questions.stem: An advantage of road transport over rail transport is that road transport
questions.explanation:
Roads reach farms, villages and homes, so goods need no transfer at either end.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- carries heavier loads: Rail carries heavier loads.
- is cheaper over very long distances: Rail and water are cheaper over long distances.
- has fewer accidents: Road has more accidents than rail.

options.label: C
options.content: is cheaper over very long distances

questions.stem: Medicines and fresh flowers are often sent by air because air transport is
questions.explanation:
Perishable, valuable and urgent goods justify the high cost of air transport.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the cheapest mode: Air transport is the most expensive.
- able to carry the heaviest loads: Aircraft carry limited, light loads.
- not affected by weather: Bad weather can delay flights.

options.label: B
options.content: able to carry the heaviest loads

questions.stem: The West African Gas Pipeline carries natural gas from
questions.explanation:
It runs from Nigeria through Benin and Togo to Ghana.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Ghana to Nigeria: Nigeria is the source of the gas.
- Senegal to Mali: This pipeline runs along the Gulf of Guinea coast.
- Sierra Leone to Guinea: Sierra Leone does not produce natural gas.

questions.stem: Lungi International Airport is separated from Freetown by
questions.explanation:
Travellers cross the estuary by ferry or water taxi, or drive a long way round.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the Loma Mountains: The Loma Mountains are in the north-east.
- the Moa River: The Moa is in the east.
- Sherbro Island: Sherbro Island is off the south coast.

papers.title: International Trade and Tourism: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on international trade and tourism, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The balance of trade of a country is the difference between
questions.explanation:
Balance of trade = visible exports − visible imports; it covers goods only.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- its total income and total spending: That describes a budget.
- its birth rate and death rate: That is natural increase.
- all its money flows with the rest of the world: That is the balance of payments.

options.label: A
options.content: its total income and total spending

options.label: B
options.content: the value of its visible exports and visible imports

options.label: C
options.content: its birth rate and death rate

options.label: D
options.content: all its money flows with the rest of the world

questions.stem: A country exports goods worth 800 million US dollars and imports goods worth 950 million US dollars. It has
questions.explanation:
800 − 950 = −150 million: imports exceed exports, an unfavourable balance.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a trade surplus of 150 million US dollars: Imports are greater than exports, so it is a deficit.
- a trade deficit of 1,750 million US dollars: That adds the values instead of subtracting.
- a balanced trade: The values are not equal.

options.label: A
options.content: a trade surplus of 150 million US dollars

options.label: B
options.content: a trade deficit of 1,750 million US dollars

options.label: C
options.content: a trade deficit of 150 million US dollars

questions.stem: The main reason why countries trade with one another is
questions.explanation:
Each country specialises in what it can produce best and buys what others produce more cheaply.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- all countries produce the same goods: If they did, there would be little reason to trade.
- every country has the same climate: Climates differ, which encourages trade.
- trade requires no transport: Trade depends on transport.

options.label: A
options.content: all countries produce the same goods

options.label: B
options.content: every country has the same climate

options.label: D
options.content: the uneven distribution of natural resources

questions.stem: Tacugama in Sierra Leone is known as
questions.explanation:
Tacugama Chimpanzee Sanctuary is in the Western Area Peninsula forest near Freetown.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- an iron-ore mine: Iron ore is mined at Tonkolili and Marampa.
- a historic slave-trading fort: That is Bunce Island.
- a hydroelectric dam: That is Bumbuna.

questions.stem: Earnings from tourism are regarded as
questions.explanation:
Tourism sells a service to foreigners, so it appears in the balance of payments, not the balance of trade.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a visible import: Tourists bring money into the country; it is not an import.
- a visible export: No goods leave the country; it is a service.
- an invisible import: Money spent by foreign tourists is earned, not spent, by the country.

papers.title: Environmental Issues and Sustainable Development: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on environmental issues and sustainable development, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Desertification in West Africa is most serious in the
questions.explanation:
Overgrazing, over-cultivation, fuelwood cutting and drought degrade the dry Sahel.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Niger Delta: The Delta is wet; its main problem is oil pollution.
- coastal mangrove belt: Mangroves grow in wet tidal areas.
- tropical rainforest: Rainforest areas suffer deforestation, not desertification.

questions.stem: The Great Green Wall project aims to
questions.explanation:
Launched by the African Union in 2007, it aims to restore degraded land across the Sahel.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- build a wall to stop sand dunes moving south: It is a planting and land-restoration project, not a wall.
- protect the rainforests of the Congo Basin: It is in the Sahel, not the Congo.
- build dams on the River Niger: It is not a dam project.

options.label: A
options.content: build a wall to stop sand dunes moving south

options.label: B
options.content: protect the rainforests of the Congo Basin

options.label: C
options.content: build dams on the River Niger

options.label: D
options.content: plant a belt of trees and restore land across the Sahel to halt desertification

questions.stem: The main greenhouse gas released by burning fossil fuels is
questions.explanation:
Carbon dioxide from burning coal, oil and gas traps heat and causes global warming.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- oxygen: Oxygen is not a greenhouse gas.
- nitrogen: Nitrogen is not a greenhouse gas.
- ozone: Burning fossil fuels mainly releases carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Sustainable development is development that
questions.explanation:
This definition comes from the Brundtland Report (1987).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- uses all resources as quickly as possible: That would leave nothing for the future.
- stops all economic growth: Sustainable development balances growth with protection.
- depends only on foreign aid: Aid is not the definition.

options.label: A
options.content: uses all resources as quickly as possible

options.label: B
options.content: meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs

questions.stem: A major effect of deforestation on steep slopes is
questions.explanation:
Without roots and cover, rain washes soil away, as in the 2017 Regent mudslide in Freetown.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- increased soil fertility: Bare soil loses nutrients and topsoil.
- more wildlife habitats: Deforestation destroys habitats.
- less flooding downstream: Faster runoff increases flooding.

papers.title: Physical Geography of Sierra Leone: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on physical geography of sierra leone, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Sierra Leone is bordered on the north and east by
questions.explanation:
Guinea lies to the north and east, Liberia to the south-east and the Atlantic to the west.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Liberia: Liberia borders Sierra Leone on the south-east.
- Côte d'Ivoire: Côte d'Ivoire does not border Sierra Leone.
- Senegal: Senegal does not border Sierra Leone.

questions.stem: The highest point in Sierra Leone is
questions.explanation:
Bintumani rises to 1,945 m in the Loma Mountains of the north-east.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Picket Hill, on the Freetown Peninsula: Picket Hill (888 m) is the highest point of the Peninsula.
- Mount Nimba: Mount Nimba is on the Guinea–Côte d'Ivoire–Liberia border.
- the Kangari Hills: The Kangari Hills are much lower.

options.label: B
options.content: Picket Hill, on the Freetown Peninsula

questions.stem: Most of the main rivers of Sierra Leone flow from
questions.explanation:
The land rises towards the north-east, so rivers such as the Rokel, Jong, Sewa and Moa flow south-west to the sea.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- south-west to north-east: Rivers flow away from the higher land in the north-east.
- west to east: The Atlantic is to the west, so rivers flow westwards.
- south to north: The rivers flow towards the Atlantic, not north.

questions.stem: The rainy season in Sierra Leone lasts from about
questions.explanation:
The moist south-west monsoon brings rain from about May to October, heaviest in July and August.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- November to April: That is the dry season.
- December to February: That is the harmattan period of the dry season.
- January to December: Sierra Leone has a distinct dry season.

questions.stem: The dry, dusty wind that blows over Sierra Leone during the dry season is the
questions.explanation:
The harmattan blows from the Sahara, especially from December to February, bringing dust and haze.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- south-west monsoon: The monsoon is moist and brings rain.
- land breeze: Land breezes are local night-time winds.
- westerlies: The westerlies blow in temperate latitudes.
